meanings.short: The three-dimensional analogue of a sphere's surface: all the points at one distance from a centre in four dimensions, finite but with no edge.
meanings.long: It is the shape of space in a closed universe. An ordinary sphere's surface is two-dimensional and sits in three-dimensional space. A 3-sphere is the same idea one dimension up: the set of points at fixed distance from a centre in four dimensions. Walking straight ahead in it brings you back where you started.

meanings.short: Of a group of operations: one in which the order does not matter, so doing A then B gives the same as B then A.
meanings.long: Named after the Norwegian mathematician Niels Henrik Abel. Phase changes of the electron field form an Abelian group, which is why electromagnetism is the simplest gauge theory.

meanings.short: Another name for the Christoffel symbols: the rule that connects directions at neighbouring points of a curved space.
meanings.long: To compare vectors at different points of a curved space you need a rule for carrying one to the other; that rule is a connection. In general relativity the connection is fixed by the metric and its components are the Christoffel symbols.

meanings.short: The antiparticle of a neutrino: emitted, for example, when a neutron decays into a proton and an electron.
meanings.long: Antineutrinos are right-handed, spinning along their direction of motion, while neutrinos are left-handed. Whether a neutrino with mass is truly different from its antiparticle is still unknown.

meanings.short: How bright an object looks from Earth: the power of its light arriving on each square metre of a detector.
meanings.long: Apparent brightness (or energy flux) falls with the square of the distance in ordinary space. In an expanding universe it also falls because of redshift, which is why astronomers use the luminosity distance.

meanings.short: The hot, dense early state of the universe, and the theory that the universe has been expanding and cooling from it ever since.
meanings.long: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe expanded and cooled from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. It explains the expansion, the cosmic microwave background and the light elements. It does not say what banged or what came before; in the simplest models the equations reach infinite density at the start, which most physicists read as a sign that the theory breaks down there.

meanings.short: The collapse at the end of a closed universe that recollapses, when all distances shrink back towards zero.
meanings.long: A closed universe of ordinary matter expands to a maximum size and then contracts, ending in a state of infinite density mirroring the Big Bang. Vacuum energy can prevent this, and our universe does not appear to be heading for one.

meanings.short: The radiation given off by a body in thermal equilibrium, whose spread over wavelengths depends only on its temperature.
meanings.long: A perfect absorber, or a cavity with a small hole, emits radiation with a universal spectrum, Planck's formula, fixed by the temperature alone. The cosmic microwave background is the best example ever measured, at 2.7 kelvin.

meanings.short: The condition of two places close enough that a signal at light speed has had time to travel between them.
meanings.long: Places out of causal contact cannot have influenced each other. In the early universe, regions out of causal contact had no way to agree on a temperature or on the state of a field.

meanings.short: A quantity built from derivatives of the metric that says how coordinate directions change from point to point, used in the geodesic equation.
meanings.long: Christoffel symbols Γ, with one upper and two lower indices, are combinations of derivatives of the metric. They vanish in Cartesian coordinates on flat space but not in polar coordinates or curved space. In the geodesic equation they play the part that gravity plays in Newton's laws.

meanings.short: A radius defined as a circle's circumference divided by 2π, used where curved space makes the ordinary radius hard to measure.
meanings.long: Near a black hole the distance to the centre is not directly measurable, but the circumference of a circle around it is. The Schwarzschild coordinate r is defined this way, so a circle at r has circumference 2πr.

everyday: Not 'old-fashioned' or 'about music': it means without quantum effects.

meanings.short: Of physics: not using quantum theory; following the laws of Newton, Maxwell and Einstein's general relativity.
meanings.long: Classical physics treats energy as continuous and empty space as empty. Many cosmological questions, such as black-body radiation and vacuum energy, can only be answered once quantum theory is included.

meanings.short: A universe with more than the critical density, whose space curves back on itself like a sphere, so it is finite.
meanings.long: In a closed universe Ω > 1 and the curvature constant k is positive. Its space is a three-dimensional sphere (a 3-sphere): finite in volume but with no edge. With matter alone it expands to a maximum size and then collapses to a Big Crunch.

meanings.short: Short for cosmic microwave background, the leftover radiation from the hot early universe.
The tiny differences, about one part in 100,000, in the temperature of the cosmic microwave background from one direction to another.
meanings.long: The pattern of these hot and cold spots, measured by COBE, WMAP and Planck, records the density ripples of the early universe. Its details fix the geometry and contents of the universe, and support both inflation and vacuum energy.

meanings.short: The Cosmic Background Explorer, a NASA satellite launched in 1989 that measured the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background.
meanings.long: COBE found the background radiation to be an almost perfect black body and, in 1992, detected its tiny variations from place to place. Two of its scientists, John Mather and George Smoot, shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

meanings.short: A small region over which the random fluctuations of a field are nearly the same, so it starts to roll everywhere together.
meanings.long: In new inflation, a coherence region that starts rolling down the plateau inflates enormously, and can become far larger than the observed universe. Different regions start rolling at different moments, so inflation ends at different times in different places.

meanings.short: A reference source of known low temperature, often cooled with liquid helium, against which a radio receiver's signal is compared.
meanings.long: Penzias and Wilson compared the hiss from their antenna with a cold load. The comparison showed the signal was real radiation from the sky and not noise in their equipment.

meanings.short: Of an infinite sum: adding up to a finite answer only when its terms are taken in a particular order; reordering can change the result.
meanings.long: A conditionally convergent series converges, but the sum of the sizes of its terms does not. The force on a mass in Newton's infinite uniform universe is like this: its value depends on the order in which the distant shells are added.

meanings.short: The rule that quarks and gluons can never be pulled apart to exist alone, because the strong force between them grows with distance.
meanings.long: Pulling a quark from a meson takes so much energy that a new quark and antiquark are created, and you end up with two mesons instead of a free quark. Quarks stay bound in groups whose colour charges cancel.

meanings.short: The distance between two points measured in comoving coordinates, which stays fixed as the universe expands.
meanings.long: In an expanding universe each galaxy keeps the same coordinates, as if painted on a stretching map. The coordinate distance between them never changes; multiply it by the scale factor to get the physical distance at a given time. Guth measures coordinate distances in 'notches'.

meanings.short: The assumption that we do not occupy a special place in the universe.
meanings.long: Named after Copernicus, who moved the Earth from the centre of the universe, the principle says our view of the cosmos should be typical. Together with the observed isotropy around us, it implies that the universe is the same in every direction from every place, so homogeneous as well.

meanings.short: The distance over which a quantity stays roughly the same, or linked, from place to place.
meanings.long: Beyond the correlation length, values at two places are effectively independent. When the Higgs field settled in the early universe, its correlation length, the size of the regions where it took one value, could be no larger than the horizon distance.

meanings.short: The separation at which pairs of galaxies are twice as common as for randomly placed galaxies.
meanings.long: The galaxy correlation function measures how much more often than chance galaxies are found at a given separation. It falls with separation as a power law, and the correlation length r₀, a few megaparsecs, is where it equals one.

meanings.short: The faint glow of microwaves filling the universe, left over from when it was hot and dense, now at 2.7 kelvin.
meanings.long: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang the universe cooled enough for atoms to form and became transparent. The light released then has been stretched by the expansion into microwaves. It has an almost perfect black-body spectrum and is the same in every direction to about one part in 100,000.

meanings.short: A thin, line-like defect that some theories predict formed in the early universe, carrying enormous energy per unit length.
meanings.long: Cosmic strings would be one-dimensional topological defects: lines along which a field is trapped in its high-energy state. None has been found.

meanings.short: The time shown by clocks that move with the expansion of the universe, all synchronised so they agree everywhere.
meanings.long: Relativity says moving clocks need not agree, but in a homogeneous universe there is a natural choice: clocks at rest relative to the matter around them, set by something all observers can see, such as the temperature of the cosmic background. The time they show is cosmic time, and the age of the universe is measured in it.

meanings.short: A constant term Einstein added to his equations of gravity, equivalent to an energy density of empty space that never changes.
meanings.long: Einstein introduced the cosmological constant Λ in 1917 to allow a static universe and later dropped it. It returned when supernova measurements in 1998 showed the expansion speeding up. Today it is read as vacuum energy, whose negative pressure causes repulsive gravity.

meanings.short: The idea that a universe dominated by vacuum energy forgets its starting shape and comes to look like smooth, exponentially expanding space.
meanings.long: It can be proved for small departures from smoothness, and is believed more generally. The name echoes the saying 'black holes have no hair': they forget the details of what made them.

meanings.short: The spacetime of a universe containing only vacuum energy, which expands exponentially.
meanings.long: Found by Willem de Sitter in 1917, it is the simplest exponentially expanding universe. It has an event horizon, and inflation and our far future both look locally like it.

meanings.short: Guth's name for the parameter θ of the closed-universe solution, running from 0 at the Big Bang to 2π at the Big Crunch.
meanings.long: The scale factor and time of a closed, matter-filled universe are both written in terms of an angle θ, like a point on a rolling wheel. θ = π is the moment of maximum size. Neither θ nor the size constant α can be measured directly; they are found from the Hubble rate and the density.

meanings.short: A kind of particle mass that links a particle with a distinct antiparticle, as the electron has; for neutrinos it would need right-handed partners.
meanings.long: A massive particle must have both spin directions available. With a Dirac mass the neutrino would get them from extra right-handed neutrinos and keep lepton number conserved.

meanings.short: Dirac's picture of the vacuum as filled with electrons in every negative-energy state, a positron being a hole in this sea.
meanings.long: Dirac's equation for the electron allowed negative energies. He proposed in 1930 that all those states are already full, so electrons cannot fall into them. The picture predicted the positron, but gave the vacuum an enormous energy; modern field theory replaced it.

meanings.short: Astronomers' logarithmic measure of distance: the difference between how bright an object looks and how bright it really is, in magnitudes.
meanings.long: The distance modulus equals 5 times the base-10 logarithm of the luminosity distance divided by 10 parsecs. Each step of 5 means a tenfold change in distance.

meanings.short: A surface-like defect that forms where two regions in which a field took different values meet.
meanings.long: Domain walls in the early universe would be sheets of trapped field energy. Like monopoles and cosmic strings, they are topological defects; heavy ones would disturb the universe so much that theories predicting them are tightly limited.

everyday: Cosmologists also use 'dust' for any matter without pressure, even whole galaxies; on other pages it means real grains of dust.

meanings.short: In cosmology: matter with no pressure, whose particles move slowly compared with light.
meanings.long: Cosmologists call pressureless matter 'dust' because its particles are treated as tiny grains that only feel gravity. Galaxies scattered through the universe behave this way on large scales.

meanings.short: Tiny solid grains floating between the stars, which dim and redden light passing through them.
meanings.long: Interstellar dust absorbs and scatters blue light more than red, and glows faintly in microwaves and infrared. Astronomers must allow for it both when reading distant supernovae and when mapping the cosmic microwave background.

meanings.short: Coming from how things change in time under physical laws, rather than being assumed at the start.
meanings.long: A dynamical explanation shows how a feature arises by itself. Inflation gives one for the universe's uniformity, which the conventional Big Bang has to put in by hand as a starting condition.

meanings.short: Able to change and to take part in physics, rather than being a fixed background; of dark energy, changing with time.
meanings.long: In general relativity space itself bends and stretches, so it is dynamical rather than a fixed stage. Dynamical dark energy would be one whose density changes as the universe ages.

meanings.short: The rule that an index appearing twice in one term is summed over all its values, without writing the sum sign.
meanings.long: Einstein introduced the convention to shorten the formulas of general relativity. A product such as gᵢⱼ dxⁱ dxʲ then means the sum over all values of i and j.

meanings.short: Of the unified electromagnetic and weak forces, which at very high temperatures act as a single force.
meanings.long: The electroweak theory of Glashow, Weinberg and Salam has the symmetry group SU(2) × U(1). As the universe cooled the Higgs field broke this symmetry, leaving the separate weak force and electromagnetism we see today.

meanings.short: Einstein's principle that, in a small enough region, the effects of gravity cannot be told apart from those of acceleration.
meanings.long: A falling observer feels weightless, as if gravity were switched off; an accelerating rocket in empty space feels like gravity. Einstein built general relativity on this: locally, a freely falling frame behaves like one without gravity. Over larger regions tidal effects reveal the gravity.

meanings.short: The idea that once inflation starts it never stops everywhere: it ends in some places while continuing, and growing, in others.
meanings.long: The inflating material decays, but it expands faster than it decays, so the total inflating volume keeps growing. Each region where inflation ends becomes a pocket universe; the result is a multiverse.

origin: Greek aithēr, the bright upper air.
everyday: It has nothing to do with the chemical called ether.

meanings.short: An invisible medium once thought to fill space and to carry light waves, abandoned after Einstein's 1905 special relativity.
meanings.long: Nineteenth-century physicists assumed light, like sound, needed a medium, and that its speed c held relative to this ether. Experiments never detected motion through it, and Einstein showed it was unnecessary: the speed of light is the same for every unaccelerated observer.

meanings.short: Following the ordinary geometry taught at school, in which parallel lines never meet and a triangle's angles add up to 180°.
meanings.long: Euclidean geometry rests on the five postulates of Euclid's Elements (about 300 BC), including the parallel postulate. Euclidean space is flat: Pythagoras's theorem gives the distance between any two points.

meanings.short: A boundary beyond which events can never send signals to us, however long we wait: a horizon about the future.
meanings.long: A black hole's surface is an event horizon. An exponentially expanding universe has one too: galaxies far enough away are carried off faster than light can close the gap, so light they emit now will never arrive.

meanings.short: Expansion in which the size doubles again and again in equal times, so it grows faster and faster.
meanings.long: With constant energy density, as for vacuum energy, the Friedmann equation gives a constant expansion rate H, and the scale factor grows as e^(Ht). This is how the universe expanded during inflation, and how it is beginning to expand today.

meanings.short: The need to set a number in a theory to an extremely precise value, for no known reason, so that it matches what we see.
meanings.long: Physicists treat fine-tuning as a sign that an explanation is missing. The flatness problem and the small observed vacuum energy are both fine-tuning problems: the conventional theories work only if some quantity is chosen to many decimal places.

everyday: Not the computer security program: the name borrows the image of a wall of fire.

meanings.short: A proposed wall of high-energy particles at a black hole's horizon, which would burn up anything falling in.
meanings.long: Classical general relativity says nothing special happens to someone crossing a horizon. In 2012 some theorists argued that quantum theory might instead require a firewall there. Whether firewalls exist remains unsettled.

everyday: In a flat universe, flat does not mean thin or two-dimensional: it means not curved.

meanings.short: Of space or spacetime: not curved, so ordinary school geometry holds; parallel lines stay apart and triangles' angles add up to 180°.
meanings.long: A flat universe has zero spatial curvature (k = 0) and exactly the critical density. 'Flat' describes geometry, not shape: a flat universe is three-dimensional and may be infinite.

meanings.short: Of a potential energy curve: nearly level, so a field on it rolls only slowly.
meanings.long: New inflation needs a broad, almost level plateau in the potential energy, so that the field takes a long time to roll down and the universe has time to inflate. Guth pictures it as a broad plateau with a gentle slope.

meanings.short: A universe with exactly the critical density, whose space has no curvature and which expands forever, ever more slowly.
meanings.long: In a flat universe the density equals the critical density (Ω = 1) and the curvature constant k is zero. It sits on the borderline between closed and open universes. Observations show our universe is flat to within a fraction of a percent, which inflation explains.

meanings.short: The puzzle of why the early universe's density was so extremely close to the critical density, when any small difference grows with time.
meanings.long: Ω = 1 is an unstable balance: any departure from it grows as the universe expands. For Ω to be near 1 today, it had to equal 1 to at least 15 decimal places one second after the Big Bang (18 with today's limits). The conventional Big Bang gives no reason; inflation drives Ω towards 1.

everyday: Nothing to do with taste: it is just a label for the kind of particle.

meanings.short: One of the different kinds within a family of particles, such as the electron, muon and tau neutrinos, or the six quarks.
meanings.long: Particles of different flavours behave alike except for their masses. Neutrinos come in three flavours and can change from one to another as they travel. Quarks come in six flavours, up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top.

meanings.short: Here: one of the three kinds of dark matter (cold, warm or hot), sorted by how fast its particles moved in the early universe.
meanings.long: Hot dark matter, such as light neutrinos, moved fast enough to smooth out small structures; cold dark matter moved slowly and did not. Warm dark matter lies between.

meanings.short: A set of four numbers, one for time and three for space, that changes between moving observers the way an event's coordinates do.
meanings.long: Combining energy and momentum into a single four-vector makes their behaviour under the Lorentz transformation simple. Its 'length' in spacetime, built with the Minkowski metric, is the same for every observer: for energy and momentum it gives the rest mass.

meanings.short: Moving under gravity alone, with no other forces acting, so that an observer feels weightless.
meanings.long: In general relativity free-falling objects follow geodesics, the straightest possible paths in curved spacetime. Comoving galaxies in an expanding universe are free-falling.

meanings.short: Of a mode or motion: not excited at all, because the smallest energy it can take is far more than the typical thermal energy.
meanings.long: In quantum theory a mode of frequency ν can only take energy in steps of hν. When hν is much larger than kT, the mode almost never gets even one step, so it holds no energy. This freezing out of short wavelengths keeps black-body radiation finite.

meanings.short: A force-carrying particle with spin one, such as the photon, the gluon or the W and Z bosons.
meanings.long: In a gauge theory each force is carried by gauge bosons. The photon and gluons are massless; the W and Z bosons of the weak force get mass from the Higgs field.

meanings.short: Unchanged by a gauge transformation, a change of the fields that alters how they are described but not anything measurable.
meanings.long: In electromagnetism the potentials can be changed in certain ways without changing the electric and magnetic fields. Only gauge-invariant quantities can be measured.

meanings.short: A theory of forces in which certain changes to the fields, made independently at each point, leave all the physics unchanged.
meanings.long: Requiring this freedom, called gauge invariance, forces the theory to contain force-carrying particles. Electromagnetism is a U(1) gauge theory; the strong and weak forces are non-Abelian gauge theories. The Standard Model and grand unified theories are built this way.

meanings.short: One of three copies of the basic family of matter particles, each heavier than the last but otherwise alike.
meanings.long: The first generation (up and down quarks, electron, electron neutrino) makes up ordinary matter. The second and third repeat the pattern with heavier particles; why there are three is unknown.

origin: Greek gē, earth, and daiein, to divide: originally land surveying.

meanings.short: The straightest possible path in a curved space or spacetime: locally the shortest (or, for clocks, the longest-time) route between two points.
meanings.long: On a sphere the geodesics are great circles. In general relativity free-falling bodies and light rays follow geodesics of spacetime; gravity is the curvature that bends them.

meanings.short: The equation of motion whose solutions are geodesics, the straightest paths in a curved space or spacetime.
meanings.long: Written with the metric and its derivatives (often through Christoffel symbols), the geodesic equation gives the second derivative of each coordinate along the path. In general relativity it is the equation of motion of a free-falling particle.

meanings.short: The massless particle that carries the strong force between quarks, as the photon carries the electromagnetic force.
meanings.long: There are eight gluons, one for each kind of SU(3) colour change. They carry the colour charge of their own force, so, unlike photons, they interact with each other.

meanings.short: The flaw of Guth's original inflation model: it could not end smoothly, leaving a jumble of bubbles instead of a uniform universe.
meanings.long: In old inflation, inflation ends as bubbles of normal vacuum form at random in the false vacuum. The space between them keeps expanding so fast that the bubbles never join up. New inflation solved this.

meanings.short: A theory in which the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces are parts of one force, which split apart as the universe cooled.
meanings.long: Grand unified theories place the three forces of the Standard Model in a single simple group such as SU(5). The unification would show only at enormous energies, around 10¹⁶ GeV. They predict magnetic monopoles and the decay of the proton; none of their predictions has yet been confirmed.

meanings.short: The energy a body has because of where it sits in a gravitational field, which turns into kinetic energy as it falls.
meanings.long: For two masses it equals −GMm/r, negative because they would have to be given energy to separate. In an expanding universe the kinetic energy of expansion and the gravitational potential energy together decide whether expansion goes on forever.

meanings.short: Short for grand unified theory.
The very high energy, about 10¹⁶ GeV, at which grand unified theories expect the three forces to merge.
meanings.long: The GUT scale is about a trillion times the energies reached by the largest particle accelerators. The early universe was this hot only a tiny fraction of a second after the Big Bang.

meanings.short: Anything that swings back and forth about a balance point with a restoring force proportional to how far it is pulled away, like a spring.
meanings.long: A harmonic oscillator has one natural frequency, whatever its amplitude. Masses on springs, pendulums at small swings and electrical circuits behave this way, and so does each mode of a wave in a box.

meanings.short: The direction of a particle's spin compared with its direction of motion: along it (right-handed) or against it (left-handed).
meanings.long: For a massless particle helicity is the same for every observer, a Lorentz-invariant label. Neutrinos are seen only with left-handed helicity and antineutrinos only with right-handed.

meanings.short: The particle of the Higgs field, discovered at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012.
meanings.long: The Higgs boson has a mass of about 125 GeV. Its discovery confirmed the Standard Model's account of how particles get mass.

meanings.short: A field filling all of space whose non-zero value today gives mass to many particles and breaks the symmetry between forces.
meanings.long: In the hot early universe the Higgs field sat at zero and the weak and electromagnetic forces looked alike. As the universe cooled it settled into a non-zero value, picking out a direction and splitting the forces apart. Its particle is the Higgs boson.

meanings.short: One of the two teams of astronomers whose observations of distant supernovae showed in 1998 that the universe's expansion is speeding up.
meanings.long: Led by Brian Schmidt, with Adam Riess as lead author of the discovery paper; 'High-Z' means high redshift. Schmidt and Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics with Saul Perlmutter of the Supernova Cosmology Project.

meanings.short: Expansion in which all distances grow by the same factor at the same time, so every place sees the same pattern.
meanings.long: In homogeneous expansion the universe is like a picture being enlarged: every distance between galaxies is multiplied by the same scale factor. Whichever galaxy you stand on, the others move away with speeds proportional to their distances, which is Hubble's law. No galaxy is the centre.

meanings.short: Of a black hole: the surface at the Schwarzschild radius; anything that falls inside can never get out again.
In cosmology: the limit of how far we can see, set by how far light has travelled since the Big Bang.
meanings.long: Light has had only a finite time to travel, so we can receive signals only from within the horizon distance. Regions farther apart than this could not yet have influenced each other.

meanings.short: The present distance of the farthest objects whose light has had time to reach us since the Big Bang.
meanings.long: Light emitted near the start travelled through a smaller, younger universe that has stretched since, so the horizon distance is larger than the speed of light times the age: three times as large in a flat, matter-only universe. It limits how far apart two places can be and still have influenced each other.

meanings.short: The puzzle of why the cosmic microwave background has the same temperature in all directions, though those regions were never in contact.
meanings.long: In the conventional Big Bang theory, when the background radiation was released, points on opposite sides of our sky were about 46 horizon distances apart, so nothing could have evened out their temperatures. Inflation solves the problem: before inflation the regions were close enough to come into equilibrium.

meanings.short: The galaxy in which a supernova or other object lies.
meanings.long: Supernovae in different kinds of host galaxy might differ slightly, so astronomers check that the brightness of type Ia supernovae does not depend on their host. Light from the host galaxy must also be subtracted to measure the supernova itself.

everyday: It is not constant in time: the rate changes as the universe ages, and H₀ is its value today.

meanings.short: Today's expansion rate of the universe: how much faster a galaxy recedes for each extra unit of distance, in km/s per megaparsec.
meanings.long: The Hubble constant H₀ is the ratio of a galaxy's recession speed to its distance today, roughly 67 to 73 km/s per megaparsec. It is 'constant' only in the sense that it is the same everywhere in space at one time; the expansion rate itself changes as the universe ages. Its inverse sets the rough age of the universe.

meanings.short: How fast the universe is expanding at a given time: the rate of growth of distances divided by the distances themselves.
meanings.long: The Hubble expansion rate H(t) equals the rate of change of the scale factor divided by the scale factor. At any one time it is the same everywhere; its value today is the Hubble constant. It decreases as gravity slows a matter-filled universe, and approaches a constant once vacuum energy dominates.

meanings.short: The motion of galaxies away from each other caused by the expansion of the universe alone, without their own extra motions.
meanings.long: In the Hubble flow every object moves away from every other with a velocity proportional to the distance between them. Real galaxies add small 'peculiar' motions of their own, caused by the pull of their neighbours, on top of this flow.

meanings.short: The speed of light divided by the Hubble expansion rate: the distance light travels in one Hubble time.
meanings.long: The Hubble length c/H is the natural length scale of an expanding universe at a given time. Today it is about 14 billion light-years. During inflation, regions much larger than the Hubble length lose contact with each other.

meanings.short: The disagreement, grown since 2013 beyond the stated errors, between the Hubble constant from nearby galaxies and that from the cosmic microwave background.
meanings.long: Measurements using Cepheid stars and supernovae give about 73 km/s per megaparsec, while fits to the cosmic microwave background give about 67. A smaller gap already showed in 2013; since then it has grown larger than the stated uncertainties. Whether it points to new physics or to hidden errors is still open; it is a later development, not part of the 2013 lectures.

meanings.short: One divided by the Hubble expansion rate: the rough time scale over which the universe changes size noticeably.
meanings.long: The Hubble time 1/H would be the age of the universe if it had always expanded at today's rate. Today it is about 14 billion years. The true age differs by a factor of order one, depending on what the universe contains: two thirds of it for a flat universe of matter alone.

meanings.short: The rule that galaxies move away from us with speeds proportional to their distances: twice as far, twice as fast.
meanings.long: Hubble's law says recession velocity equals the Hubble constant times distance. It holds for galaxies far enough away that their own random motions are small compared with the expansion. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended calling it the Hubble–Lemaître law, because Lemaître derived and estimated it in 1927, two years before Hubble published.

meanings.short: Of geometry: curved like a saddle, so many parallels pass through a point and a triangle's angles add up to less than 180°.
meanings.long: Hyperbolic geometry, found by Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky, keeps all of Euclid's postulates except the parallel postulate. It is the geometry of space in an open universe.

meanings.short: Of functions: the hyperbolic sine and cosine, sinh and cosh, built from exponentials as cousins of the ordinary sine and cosine.
meanings.long: sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2. They replace sine and cosine in the solution for an open universe, because the curvature there is negative.

meanings.short: A clock that runs at the rate of an unaccelerated clock moving alongside it, so its rate depends only on its speed.
meanings.long: Real clocks are damaged by violent acceleration. Physicists define an ideal clock as one whose rate at each moment equals that of an unaccelerated clock at the same speed. Such a clock measures proper time along its path.

meanings.short: The theory that the very early universe went through a brief burst of extremely fast, exponential expansion, driven by repulsive gravity.
meanings.long: Proposed by Guth in 1980, the inflationary universe theory adds a short period before the conventional Big Bang. It explains why the universe is so uniform, so flat and so free of monopoles, and its quantum fluctuations seed the galaxies.

meanings.short: The field, or its particle, whose energy drives inflation; probably not the Higgs field, though modelled on it.
meanings.long: While the inflaton sits in a high-energy state, such as a false vacuum, it acts like vacuum energy and makes the universe inflate. When it rolls down to its lowest energy, inflation ends and its energy is released as particles.

meanings.short: The failure of classical physics to explain cavity radiation: it predicts infinite energy at short wavelengths.
meanings.long: Classical physics gives every mode of the radiation in a box the same average energy kT, and there are infinitely many short-wavelength modes. The paradox, also called the ultraviolet catastrophe, was resolved by Planck's quantum hypothesis.

meanings.short: A choice of coordinates for a black hole spacetime that shows nothing singular happens at the horizon.
meanings.long: In the usual Schwarzschild coordinates the formulas blow up at the Schwarzschild radius. Kruskal coordinates (1960) cover the horizon smoothly, showing the trouble was in the coordinates, not in spacetime; the real singularity is at the centre.

everyday: No scenery: the word pictures the energy of each possible vacuum as the height of a hilly countryside.

meanings.short: The huge range of possible vacuum states that string theory allows, each with its own physical constants.
meanings.long: Estimates once put the number of string theory vacua around 10⁵⁰⁰. Pictured as hills and valleys of energy, the landscape suggests the laws we observe may be local features of our pocket universe.

meanings.short: Of a set of axes or a turning: the mirror image of the usual right-handed one, matching the curled fingers of a left hand.
meanings.long: Swapping two axes of a right-handed coordinate system gives a left-handed one. Mirror images change handedness.

meanings.short: Of a particle: spinning in the opposite direction to its motion, like a left-handed screw.
meanings.long: All neutrinos seen in experiments are left-handed; antineutrinos are right-handed. A massless particle's handedness is the same for every observer.

meanings.short: A particle that does not feel the strong force, such as the electron, the muon, the tau and the neutrinos.
meanings.long: There are six leptons, in three generations: each charged lepton (electron, muon, tau) has its own neutrino. Leptons are fermions, with spin one half.

meanings.short: A count of leptons minus antileptons, which all observed reactions leave unchanged.
meanings.long: Each lepton counts plus one and each antilepton minus one; in fact each flavour (electron, muon, tau) has its own number, conserved apart from neutrino oscillations. A Majorana mass for neutrinos would break lepton number, which is how experiments try to tell the two kinds of mass apart.

meanings.short: The lightest atomic nuclei, mainly hydrogen, helium and a little lithium, most of which were made in the first minutes after the Big Bang.
meanings.long: Heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen were made much later in stars. The amounts of the light elements are a key test of the Big Bang theory.

meanings.short: Of two events: separated so that light could just travel from one to the other; the interval between them is zero.
meanings.long: The interval between events sorts them into three kinds: timelike (a slower-than-light traveller could attend both), spacelike (nothing could), and lightlike, the borderline, also called null. Light rays follow lightlike paths.

meanings.short: Looking like ordinary flat geometry over small enough regions, even if the space is curved on a large scale.
meanings.long: The Earth's surface is curved, yet a town map works with flat geometry. In the same way any smooth curved space looks Euclidean close up; Riemann's geometry is built on this idea.

meanings.short: Unchanged when you switch between observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other.
meanings.long: A quantity is Lorentz invariant if every unaccelerated observer computes the same value for it, even though they disagree about times and distances. The spacetime interval, the speed of light and a particle's rest mass are examples.

meanings.short: A value that a quantity is known to be at least: the true value cannot be smaller.
meanings.long: A lower bound need not be the true value, only a floor beneath it. For example, 'the energy has a lower bound of zero' means it is never negative.

meanings.short: The distance an object would need, in ordinary static space, for its known true brightness to give the brightness we measure.
meanings.long: Luminosity distance is defined so that apparent brightness equals luminosity divided by 4π times its square. In an expanding universe it depends on the redshift and on what the universe contains, which is how supernovae measure the expansion history.

meanings.short: The magnetic counterpart of electric charge: a source from which magnetic field lines spread out, as they do from an electric charge.
meanings.long: Maxwell's equations as usually written say there is none: magnetic field lines have no beginning or end. A magnetic monopole would carry magnetic charge; Dirac showed it would have to come in fixed units.

meanings.short: A particle with a single magnetic pole, north or south alone, carrying magnetic charge, predicted by grand unified theories but never found.
meanings.long: Ordinary magnets always have two poles. Grand unified theories predict extremely heavy monopoles, about 10¹⁶ times the proton's mass, formed as knots in the Higgs field when the universe cooled.

meanings.short: The puzzle that grand unified theories predict a huge number of heavy monopoles from the early universe, yet none are seen.
meanings.long: Estimates in the conventional Big Bang give far too many monopoles: their mass would close the universe many times over. Inflation solves the problem by spreading them so thinly that we would not expect to see even one.

meanings.short: A kind of particle mass possible only for neutral particles, which makes the particle its own antiparticle.
meanings.long: If neutrinos have Majorana masses, the right-handed 'antineutrino' is simply the other spin state of the neutrino, and lepton number is not exactly conserved. Experiments searching for neutrinoless double beta decay test this.

everyday: Everyday matter is any stuff; in cosmology the word excludes radiation and vacuum energy.

meanings.short: In cosmology: particles moving much slower than light, so they exert almost no pressure; ordinary matter and dark matter, as opposed to radiation.
meanings.long: Cosmologists divide the contents of the universe into matter (non-relativistic particles, whose energy density falls as 1/a³), radiation (falling as 1/a⁴) and vacuum energy (constant). Matter dominated the universe from about 50,000 years after the Big Bang until a few billion years ago.

meanings.short: Of a universe or era: one in which matter supplies most of the energy density, so it controls the expansion.
meanings.long: In a flat matter-dominated universe the scale factor grows as the two-thirds power of time. Our universe was matter-dominated from about 50,000 years after the Big Bang until a few billion years ago.

meanings.short: A million parsecs, about 3.26 million light-years: the usual unit for distances between galaxies.
meanings.long: One megaparsec (Mpc) is about 3.09 × 10²² metres. The Hubble constant is usually quoted in kilometres per second per megaparsec: the extra speed of recession for each megaparsec of distance.

origin: Greek meta, beyond, and Latin stabilis, steady.

meanings.short: Stable against small disturbances but not permanently, because a lower-energy state exists that it can eventually reach.
meanings.long: A ball in a dip on a hillside is metastable: small nudges do not move it, but a big enough push, or quantum tunnelling, lets it escape to the valley below. A false vacuum is metastable.

meanings.short: Here: lasting long but not for ever; on a gentle plateau the field is only balanced, and the smallest nudge sets it rolling slowly.
meanings.long: On the plateau of new inflation the false vacuum has no barrier to hold it. It survives a long time only because the slope is so gentle that rolling off takes many doubling times.

meanings.short: The rule for the interval between two events in flat spacetime, with no gravity: space parts enter with one sign, time with the other.
meanings.long: In Cartesian coordinates the Minkowski metric gives ds² = −c²dt² + dx² + dy² + dz² (or the same with all signs reversed). It is the spacetime of special relativity, and the local form of every spacetime in general relativity.

meanings.short: Short for multicolour light-curve shape: a method that corrects a type Ia supernova's brightness using how its light rises and fades in several colours.
meanings.long: Brighter type Ia supernovae fade more slowly. The High-Z team used this pattern, measured on nearby supernovae, to turn each light curve into a corrected peak brightness and so a distance.

meanings.short: A collection of many universes or pocket universes, which may have different physical laws or constants.
meanings.long: Eternal inflation suggests a multiverse of pocket universes. Combined with the many possible vacua of string theory, it is used to argue that our vacuum's small energy might be a selection effect. The idea is speculative and hard to test.

meanings.short: A pressure that pulls inwards, like tension in a stretched rubber sheet, rather than pushing outwards.
meanings.long: Vacuum energy has a pressure equal to minus its energy density. In general relativity pressure, as well as energy, creates gravity, and a large enough negative pressure makes gravity repulsive. This drives inflation and today's accelerating expansion.

meanings.short: A very light, electrically neutral particle that feels only the weak interaction and gravity, so it passes through almost anything.
meanings.long: Neutrinos come in three flavours, linked to the electron, muon and tau. They were once thought massless; oscillations between flavours show at least two have small masses. The early universe left a background of neutrinos, slightly colder than the cosmic microwave background.

meanings.short: The improved inflation model of 1982 (Linde; Albrecht and Steinhardt), in which the field rolls slowly off a broad, flat plateau.
meanings.long: Because the field rolls instead of tunnelling, inflation ends smoothly and almost uniformly over a whole region, solving the graceful exit problem. It was proposed in 1982 by Andrei Linde and, independently, by Andreas Albrecht and Paul Steinhardt.

meanings.short: Of a group of operations: one in which the order matters, so doing A then B can differ from B then A, as with rotations.
meanings.long: Yang and Mills built the first non-Abelian gauge theories in 1954. The strong and weak forces are of this kind; their force carriers interact with each other, unlike photons.

meanings.short: Of geometry: one in which the parallel postulate fails, so space is curved, as on a sphere or a saddle.
meanings.long: Non-Euclidean geometries were found in the nineteenth century by dropping Euclid's parallel postulate. On a sphere no parallels exist and triangles' angles add up to more than 180°; in hyperbolic geometry there are many and the angles add up to less.

meanings.short: Guth's name for the arbitrary unit of comoving coordinates in 8.286, so the scale factor is measured in metres per notch.
meanings.long: Comoving coordinates can be marked off in any unit; Guth calls it a notch to stress that the choice is arbitrary. The scale factor then has units of metres per notch, and the curvature constant k units of one per notch squared. Every physical answer comes out independent of the notch, which is a useful check on a calculation.

origin: Latin nucleus, kernel, and Greek synthesis, putting together.

meanings.short: The making of atomic nuclei; in cosmology, the forming of the light elements in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
meanings.long: Big Bang nucleosynthesis turned about a quarter of the protons and neutrons into helium-4, with traces of deuterium, helium-3 and lithium. The predicted amounts agree with those measured, and depend on how fast the universe was expanding, which makes them a test of the theory.

meanings.short: A universe with less than the critical density, whose space curves like a saddle and which expands forever.
meanings.long: In an open universe Ω < 1 and the curvature constant k is negative. Its space is the hyperbolic geometry of Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky, and it is infinite. Gravity is too weak to stop the expansion.

meanings.short: Guth's first model of inflation (1980), in which the field was trapped in a dip of its potential and escaped by quantum tunnelling.
meanings.long: Also called old inflation. It does not work, because the tunnelling makes scattered bubbles that never merge: the graceful exit problem.

meanings.short: Euclid's fifth assumption: through a point not on a given line exactly one line can be drawn that never meets it.
meanings.long: For two thousand years mathematicians tried to prove the parallel postulate from Euclid's other four. In the nineteenth century they found that it can be false: dropping it gives consistent non-Euclidean geometries.

meanings.short: A solution that gives two quantities, such as size and time, each as a function of a third helper variable, instead of one directly.
meanings.long: The Friedmann equation for a closed universe cannot be solved for the scale factor as a simple function of time. Instead both are written in terms of the development angle θ: ct = α(θ − sin θ) and a/√k = α(1 − cos θ), the equations of a cycloid.

meanings.short: A unit of distance used in astronomy, about 3.26 light-years or 3.09 × 10¹⁶ metres.
meanings.long: A star one parsec away shifts back and forth on the sky by one second of arc as the Earth goes round the Sun: the name joins 'parallax' and 'second'. Astronomers use it, and its multiples the kiloparsec and megaparsec, for distances to stars and galaxies.

meanings.short: The boundary of the region from which light could have reached us since the beginning: a horizon about the past.
meanings.long: The particle horizon is the horizon distance seen as a surface around the observer. It concerns the past; an event horizon concerns the future. The horizons in the horizon problem are particle horizons.

origin: Greek phainomenon, that which appears, and logos, study.

meanings.short: The description of how something behaves and what effects it has, without an explanation of what it is underneath.
meanings.long: Guth says the phenomenology of dark energy is understood: it acts like vacuum energy. What is not understood is why the vacuum has the energy it does.

meanings.short: The hypothetical partner of the photon in supersymmetry: a particle with spin one half instead of spin one.
meanings.long: Supersymmetry predicts it but no experiment has found it. If it existed and were the lightest such particle, it could be a dark matter candidate.

meanings.short: The distance between two points as rulers would measure it at one moment of cosmic time, which grows as the universe expands.
meanings.long: The physical distance equals the scale factor times the coordinate distance. It is the distance you would find by laying rulers end to end between two galaxies, all at the same cosmic time, with each ruler at rest relative to the matter around it.

meanings.short: A tiny length, about 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ metres, below which quantum effects of gravity are expected to matter.
meanings.long: The Planck length is built from Planck's constant, Newton's constant and the speed of light. Physics as we know it is not expected to hold at smaller distances.

meanings.short: One of the many regions where inflation has ended, each looking from inside like a whole universe with its own Big Bang.
meanings.long: In eternal inflation our observed universe would be one pocket universe among infinitely many. Each may be enormous; 'pocket' only means it is one of many.

meanings.short: The equation linking a potential to its source: for gravity, the density of mass; for electricity, the density of charge.
meanings.long: For gravity, Poisson's equation says the Laplacian of the gravitational potential equals 4πG times the mass density: the field form of Newton's law. Guth uses it to show why Newton's infinite static universe is ambiguous. [Guth sometimes calls it Laplace's equation, which is the special case with zero density.]

meanings.short: The time measured by a clock carried along with a moving object, which all observers agree on.
meanings.long: Proper time is the time ticked off by an ideal clock along its own path through spacetime. Different observers disagree about coordinate times, but they all compute the same proper time between two events on the clock's path, from the spacetime interval.

meanings.short: Like a Riemannian geometry, except that the squared distance between nearby points can be negative, as in the geometry of spacetime.
meanings.long: Spacetime's metric has three positive signs for space and one negative for time (or the reverse). The squared interval between two events can then be positive, negative or zero. Such a geometry is called pseudo-Riemannian.

meanings.short: A small, random variation in a field that quantum theory says must happen even in its lowest-energy state.
meanings.long: During inflation, quantum fluctuations of the inflaton were stretched to astronomical sizes. They left tiny differences in density, about one part in 100,000, which gravity later grew into galaxies.

origin: Latin quinta essentia, the fifth essence: the substance of the heavens in ancient thought.

meanings.short: A proposed kind of dark energy made by a slowly changing field, whose energy density, unlike vacuum energy, could change over time.
meanings.long: Quintessence would behave much like a cosmological constant today, but could change slowly. Hints from surveys since 2024 that dark energy might change have made it a live question, though the simplest quintessence models do not fit the data well either.

everyday: It does not mean harmful radioactivity: here it means light and other fast particles.

meanings.short: In cosmology: particles moving at or near the speed of light, such as photons and neutrinos, whose energy density falls fastest as the universe expands.
meanings.long: The energy density of radiation falls as 1/a⁴: the number of particles is diluted by the volume, and each one loses energy to redshift. Radiation therefore dominated the early universe, until about 50,000 years after the Big Bang.

meanings.short: The radius of the circle or sphere that best matches a curve or a curved space: the larger it is, the gentler the bend.
meanings.long: A circle of radius R bends at the same rate everywhere; any smooth curve can be matched near a point by such a circle. For a closed universe the radius of curvature is the scale factor divided by the square root of k: the radius of the 3-sphere. A space whose radius of curvature is much larger than the region we can see looks flat to us.

everyday: Despite 're', electrons and nuclei had never been combined before: the name comes from laboratory physics.

meanings.short: The joining of electrons and nuclei into neutral hydrogen atoms as the early universe cooled below about 4,000 kelvin.
meanings.long: Before recombination the universe was a hot plasma that light could not cross. Guth dates it to the time when half the hydrogen had become neutral, at about 4,000 K. Light stopped scattering a little later, at decoupling (about 3,000 K, some 380,000 years after the Big Bang), and that light is the cosmic microwave background.

meanings.short: A stretching of light to longer wavelengths, so lines in a spectrum appear shifted towards the red.
meanings.long: Redshift z is defined by 1 + z = the observed wavelength divided by the emitted wavelength. It is caused by a source moving away (the Doppler effect), by climbing out of gravity, or, for distant galaxies, by the expansion of space while the light travelled: then 1 + z equals the ratio of the scale factor now to the scale factor at emission.

meanings.short: The heating of the universe at the end of inflation, when the inflaton's energy is turned into a hot gas of particles.
meanings.long: During inflation everything else is diluted to almost nothing. When the inflaton decays, its energy fills the universe with particles at a temperature comparable to the energy scale of the theory; that hot gas is the starting point of the conventional Big Bang.

meanings.short: An older name for a moving particle's total energy divided by c², which grows with its speed.
meanings.long: Relativistic mass equals the rest mass multiplied by the Lorentz factor. Most physicists now avoid the term and speak of energy instead; in cosmology it is a reminder that the energy of moving particles, including the energy of radiation, contributes to gravity.

meanings.short: The fact, from special relativity, that two events at the same time for one observer can happen at different times for another.
meanings.long: Observers moving relative to each other slice spacetime into 'now' differently. Two distant events that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving along the line joining them. This is why a universal time has to be defined with care in cosmology.

meanings.short: Gravity that pushes things apart instead of pulling them together, caused in general relativity by a large negative pressure.
meanings.long: Material with negative pressure, such as vacuum energy or a false vacuum, produces gravitational repulsion. It is not ordinary gravity reversed: it acts on everything alike and makes the expansion of the universe speed up.

meanings.short: The mass of a particle measured by an observer at rest relative to it, the same for every observer.
meanings.long: Rest mass is the invariant mass of special relativity. A particle's energy is its rest energy (rest mass times c²) plus its kinetic energy. Photons have zero rest mass, so they always move at the speed of light.

meanings.short: Of a geometry: one in which distances are given by a metric that varies from place to place, and which is Euclidean close up.
meanings.long: Bernhard Riemann described curved spaces of any dimension by a metric, a rule giving the distance between nearby points. In a Riemannian space the squared distance is always positive; general relativity uses the pseudo-Riemannian variant for spacetime.

meanings.short: The formula for distances in space and time in a universe that is the same everywhere and in every direction.
meanings.long: The Robertson–Walker metric contains the scale factor a(t) and the curvature constant k, which covers closed, flat and open universes. Any homogeneous and isotropic universe can be described by it. With the Friedmann equations, which fix a(t), it is the basis of standard cosmology.

meanings.short: The radius 2GM/c² of the horizon of a non-rotating black hole of mass M; nothing inside can get out.
meanings.long: For the Sun the Schwarzschild radius is about 3 kilometres, for the Earth about 9 millimetres. A body squeezed inside its Schwarzschild radius must collapse into a black hole.

meanings.short: A bias caused by the way observations are chosen or made possible, so what we see is not typical of the whole.
meanings.long: We live where the density is about that of water, though the universe on average is far emptier, simply because life needs dense matter. The anthropic argument uses the same kind of reasoning about which vacuum we find ourselves in.

meanings.short: The hypothetical partner of the electron in supersymmetry: a particle with spin zero instead of spin one half.
meanings.long: Supersymmetry predicts it but no experiment has found it. If it exists it must be much heavier than the electron.

meanings.short: Space and time together, treated as one four-dimensional whole in which each event has a place and a time.
meanings.long: Relativity joins space and time because observers in different states of motion split them differently. Distances in spacetime are measured by the interval, which all observers agree on. In general relativity spacetime is curved by matter and energy.

meanings.short: The way a system whose laws are symmetric can settle into a state that is not, as water freezing into crystals picks out directions.
meanings.long: The laws may treat many states alike, but the lowest-energy state has to pick one. When the Higgs field settled, the symmetry between the weak and electromagnetic forces was broken in this way, though the underlying equations keep it.

meanings.short: A kind of object whose true brightness is known, so its distance can be found from how bright it looks.
meanings.long: Comparing the known luminosity of a standard candle with its apparent brightness gives its distance by the inverse-square law. Cepheid stars and type Ia supernovae are the main standard candles of cosmology.

meanings.short: A proposed theory in which the basic particles are tiny vibrating strings, aiming to combine quantum theory and gravity.
meanings.long: String theory needs extra dimensions of space, curled up too small to see. It seems to allow an enormous number of possible vacua rather than one. It has not yet been tested by experiment.

meanings.short: The force that holds quarks together inside protons and neutrons, and holds nuclei together, carried by gluons.
meanings.long: The strong force acts on colour charge. Its strength grows as quarks are pulled apart, so quarks are never seen alone.

meanings.short: The group of 2 × 2 unitary matrices with determinant 1; in particle physics, the symmetry group of the weak force.
meanings.long: SU(2) also describes how spin one half behaves under rotations. Combined with U(1) it forms the electroweak part of the Standard Model.

meanings.short: The group of 3 × 3 unitary matrices with determinant 1; in particle physics, the symmetry group of the strong force.
meanings.long: The Standard Model's symmetry group is SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1), one factor for each of the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions. Its eight independent directions correspond to the eight gluons.

meanings.short: The group of 5 × 5 unitary matrices with determinant 1, used in the simplest grand unified theory (Georgi and Glashow, 1974).
meanings.long: SU(5) contains SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1) as a part, so a theory built on it joins the three forces of the Standard Model into one. It predicts that protons decay, which experiments have ruled out at the predicted rate.

meanings.short: The team led by Saul Perlmutter which, with the High-Z team, discovered in 1998 that the universe's expansion is speeding up.
meanings.long: Based at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the project began in 1988 to measure how fast the expansion was slowing down, and found instead that it is accelerating. Its results and those of the High-Z team agreed, which made the discovery convincing.

meanings.short: A proposed symmetry giving every matter particle (spin one half) a partner with whole-number spin, and every force carrier a partner with spin one half.
meanings.long: Supersymmetry would give each fermion a boson partner and each boson a fermion partner, such as the photino and the selectron. In an exactly supersymmetric theory the vacuum energy would be zero. No partner particle has been found, so if supersymmetry exists it must be broken.

meanings.short: A state in which energy is shared out evenly and nothing changes on average, so the system can be described by a single temperature.
meanings.long: Two systems in thermal equilibrium exchange no net heat. In the early universe particles collided so often that they stayed in thermal equilibrium as the universe expanded, which is why the cosmic background radiation has a black-body spectrum.

meanings.short: The stretching and squeezing caused by gravity pulling differently on different parts of an object.
meanings.long: Because gravity weakens with distance, the side of a body nearer the source is pulled harder than the far side. This difference raises the ocean tides and, near a small black hole, would tear an object apart. Tidal effects cannot be removed by free fall, which is how gravity shows itself in a falling frame.

meanings.short: The slowing of a moving clock as seen by an observer it moves past, predicted by special relativity.
meanings.long: A clock moving at speed v ticks more slowly, by a factor of the square root of one minus v²/c², than the clocks of the observer it passes. The effect is real and measured: fast unstable particles live longer, and it is one ingredient of the relativistic Doppler shift.

meanings.short: A flaw that is frozen into a field when it settles in different ways in different regions, such as a monopole, string or wall.
meanings.long: When the universe cooled, a field like the Higgs could settle into different states in regions out of contact. Where those regions meet, the field may be unable to settle smoothly, leaving a defect: a point (monopole), line (cosmic string) or surface (domain wall).

meanings.short: A method of solving an integral by replacing the variable with a sine, cosine or similar function so that a square root simplifies.
meanings.long: When an integrand contains a square root such as √(1 − x²) or √(x(2 − x)), substituting x = sin θ or x = 1 − cos θ turns the root into a single trigonometric function. Guth uses this to integrate the Friedmann equation for a closed universe.

everyday: Nothing is dug: the object simply turns up on the other side of a barrier.

meanings.short: In quantum physics: to pass through an energy barrier that classical physics says cannot be crossed, with a small probability.
meanings.long: Quantum objects are described by waves that leak a little way into forbidden regions. So a particle, or a whole field such as a false vacuum, can appear on the other side of a barrier without ever having the energy to climb over it.

meanings.short: The explosion of a white dwarf star, which reaches nearly the same peak brightness every time and so serves as a standard candle.
meanings.long: A type Ia supernova occurs when a white dwarf gains mass from a companion and is blown apart by runaway nuclear burning. Its peak brightness, corrected using how fast it fades, is nearly the same everywhere. Two teams used them in 1998 to show that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

meanings.short: The group of multiplications by a phase, a complex number of size one; the gauge symmetry of electromagnetism.
meanings.long: U(1) stands for the unitary 1 × 1 matrices: complex numbers e^(iθ). Changing the phase of a field by a different amount at each point is the gauge symmetry of electromagnetism. The U(1) factor of the Standard Model's SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1) is a close relative, called hypercharge; electromagnetism's U(1) is what survives after the Higgs field breaks the electroweak symmetry.

meanings.short: The group of multiplications by a phase; here the equations stay unchanged when the whole field gets one common phase, which conserves particle number.
meanings.long: Because the same phase change is made everywhere, this is a global symmetry, not a gauge symmetry. It goes with a conserved quantity, the number of particles.

meanings.short: Energy that empty space itself carries, the same everywhere and unchanged as the universe expands.
meanings.long: In quantum theory the vacuum is not truly empty: fields fluctuate even in their lowest state. Its energy density acts exactly like a cosmological constant: it has a negative pressure, so its gravity is repulsive. Estimates from particle physics are wildly larger than the observed value, a famous unsolved puzzle.

meanings.short: The zero-point energy of all a field's modes in their lowest state; between two plates it depends on the gap, which causes the Casimir force.
meanings.long: Each mode of a quantum field keeps half a quantum of energy even when empty. Plates allow only certain modes between them, so the total changes with their separation, and the plates are pushed together.

meanings.short: Of a universe or era: one in which vacuum energy supplies most of the energy density, so the expansion speeds up.
meanings.long: Once vacuum energy dominates, the expansion becomes exponential. Our universe has been vacuum-dominated for the last few billion years; the standard model of this, ΛCDM, is a vacuum-dominated model.

meanings.short: The heavy force-carrying particles of the weak interaction: the charged W⁺ and W⁻ and the neutral Z⁰.
meanings.long: Discovered at CERN in 1983, they have masses of about 80 and 91 GeV, roughly 86 and 97 times the proton's mass. Their large mass, from the Higgs field, is why the weak force has such a short range.

meanings.short: The force behind some radioactive decays and all neutrino reactions, very weak at everyday energies because its carriers are heavy.
meanings.long: Neutron decay into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino is a weak process. At high energies the weak and electromagnetic forces merge into the electroweak force.

meanings.short: The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe, a NASA satellite (2001 to 2010) that mapped the cosmic microwave background across the sky.
meanings.long: WMAP followed COBE with much finer maps of the background's temperature variations, from which it measured the age, contents and geometry of the universe. The European Planck satellite followed it.

meanings.short: The standard model of cosmology: a flat universe containing a cosmological constant (Λ), cold dark matter and ordinary matter.
meanings.long: ΛCDM, said 'lambda C D M', fits the supernova data, the cosmic microwave background and the clustering of galaxies with a handful of numbers. In it about 70 per cent of today's energy density is vacuum energy and about 25 per cent dark matter.
